summary:
RockIT provides tools to make NASA's Earth data accessible and understandable. The RockIT web application provides an analysis of variations in temperature at the surface of the Earth, precipitation, soil moisture, and evapotranspiration over 21 regions between 2001 and 2024 based on estimates provided by NASA GLDAS land surface model.

The users choose regions on a globe, compare historical observations and observe trends that show uncertainties and evidence indicators. Date range is set individually; it triggers new statistical analysis. We provide a trained, unsupervised machine learning classifier that clusters regions based on their fingerprints of change in four variables, and Earth Twins finds regions with a similar pattern over time even across different continents.

RockIT links research and transparency: users are able to explore seasonal patterns, evaluate results, learn about limitations, and download our analysis. Created for students, teachers and curious minds, it transforms complex Earth data into simple questions: What changed? How strong is the evidence? And where else something similar happened?
details:
From a globe to evidence

Earth data can reveal important patterns, but downloading scientific files, defining geographic regions, accounting for seasons, and interpreting uncertainty can create barriers to exploration. RockIT brings those steps together in an interactive Earth trend detective.

Our application explores NASA GLDAS Noah version 2.1 monthly land-surface estimates from January 2001 through December 2024. It covers 21 predefined study regions and four connected environmental variables: surface temperature, precipitation, upper-layer soil moisture, and evapotranspiration. The processed dataset contains 24,192 regional monthly values.

How it works

Our extraction pipeline calculates regional averages using the area of intersection between NASA grid cells and documented geographic boundaries. This gives partially intersecting cells an appropriate contribution instead of treating every cell equally. Download checkpoints and cached geographic weights make extraction resumable and more efficient.

For each region and variable, we fit a linear trend alongside calendar-month effects to account for the repeating seasonal cycle. We estimate uncertainty using a Bartlett/Newey–West covariance calculation that allows for correlated monthly residuals. Benjamini–Hochberg correction addresses multiple testing across the region-variable trend family.

Users can inspect monthly values, seasonal anomalies, annual summaries, trend estimates, approximate 95% confidence intervals, and adjusted evidence indicators. A result can remain inconclusive: RockIT does not force every record into a claim of change. Users can also choose a custom time window, which triggers a fresh statistical fit using the same method.

Discovering Earth Twins

We translate each region’s four trends into a change fingerprint by dividing each trend by that region’s monthly-anomaly variability. This allows variables with different physical units to contribute to a shared comparison.

We trained an unsupervised K-means model on 20 regional fingerprints, evaluating two through five groups using separation, group size, random-seed stability, and endpoint sensitivity. Two groups passed our project’s heuristic checks. Whole California was excluded from fitting and assigned afterward because it contains the Central Valley study region.

Earth Twins ranks regions by the distance between their fingerprints. Two distant regions can share a historical pattern of change without sharing the same climate. Additional discovery features highlight large supported trends and regions with supported changes in opposite directions.

The clustering, twin comparisons, and discovery lists describe the full 2001–2024 record. Custom date windows update the statistical analysis without silently changing the scope of those full-record patterns.

Benefits and intended impact

RockIT supports environmental data literacy by connecting an accessible globe interface with inspectable evidence. Students and educators can compare regions, investigate multiple aspects of land-surface change, and see why uncertainty matters. Curious users can move from a visual discovery to its underlying time series and download monthly data, trend tables, or complete analysis results.

Its creative element is the connection between geography, statistics, and machine learning: users investigate a place, examine the evidence for change, and discover other places with similar multidimensional fingerprints.

Tools and implementation

We used Python and Jupyter/Google Colab for extraction, analysis, and model training. Scientific and geospatial tools include NumPy, pandas, SciPy, statsmodels, scikit-learn, xarray, GeoPandas, Shapely, pyproj, and earthaccess.

A FastAPI backend serves consistent analysis bundles and calculates custom-window trends. The frontend uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and MapLibre GL. The repository includes Docker configurations and deployment instructions for Google Cloud Run. All 29 backend integration tests passed during verification, including numerical consistency checks between the notebooks, API, and saved clustering outputs.

Responsible interpretation

RockIT analyzes historical GLDAS model estimates. It does not establish causation or forecast future conditions. Regions differ in size and type, and some overlap. Confidence intervals do not capture all uncertainty in the underlying modelling system, and similarity results remain exploratory. Scientific review is ongoing, and an unusually step-like temperature series is explicitly flagged for further investigation.
